titleEn: The Song of the Cid — The moneylenders pay; the Cid leaves Burgos for San Pedro de Cardeña (tiradas 10–14, lines 174–241)
part: Tiradas 10–14 · The moneylenders pay; the Cid leaves Burgos for San Pedro de Cardeña (lines 174–241)

sentences.t:
Raquel a mio Çid la manol [h]a besa[da]:
“¡Ya Canpeador, en buen[a] cinxiestes espada!
de Castiella vos ides pora las yentes estrañas.
sentences.l:
Raquel to my Çid the-hand-to-him has kissed:
“O Campeador, in a-good (hour) you-girded sword!
from Castile yourself you-go toward the peoples foreign.
sentences.i: Raquel kissed my Çid's hand: “O Campeador, in a good hour you girded on your sword! You are going out of Castile to foreign peoples.
sentences.n: Tirada 10 (assonance á-a) — the Çid promises Raquel a Moorish fur; the lenders count out the six hundred marks at their house in Burgos, and Martín Antolínez asks for his fee. Every line-ending of the tirada carries á-a (besada, espada, estrañas … arcas, calças), and none falls outside it. manol = mano + l(e), 'the hand to him': the enclitic squeeze again, the pronoun glued to the noun as in ferídal at v. 38. [h]a besa[da] is aver + past participle, with the participle still agreeing with its object (la mano, feminine), as in ovo bastidos at v. 68; the h and the -da are Pidal's restorations. Raquel speaks alone here, for once apart from Vidas. en buen[a] cinxiestes espada is the sword-form of the honorific formula, word for word the girl's greeting at v. 41 (there spelt çinxiestes); cinxiestes is the strong preterite of çeñir, second person plural used respectfully to one man. vos ides = os vais, 'you are going away' (ir with the reflexive, 2nd pl. present). yentes estrañas = foreign peoples, the lands beyond Castile.

sentences.i: Such is your fortune, and great are your gains: a fine crimson Moorish fur — Çid, I kiss your hand, that I may have it as a gift.”
sentences.n: The request is the reason for the speech: a broker's courtesy-gift for the pawning. piel here is a fur-lined robe or cloak, not a raw skin (the alcándaras of v. 4 stood empty of pielles); vermeja = bermeja, the costly scarlet; morisca = of Moorish make, exactly what a man going to the frontier might bring back. ondrada = honrada, 'fine, worthy of honour'. Kissing the hand is the gesture that asks a boon of a lord. que la yo aya: aya is the present subjunctive of aver, 'that I may have it'; Old Spanish can set the subject yo between the object pronoun la and its verb, an order modern Spanish does not allow. Raquel speaks of ganancias as if the Çid's future booty were already counted, and takes his exile for a business venture.

sentences.t:
—“Plazme”, dixo el Çid, “daquí sea mandada.
Si vos la aduxier dallá; si non, contalda sobre las arcas.”
sentences.l:
—“It-pleases-me”, said the Çid, “from-here let-it-be promised.
If to-you it I-bring from-there; if not, count-it upon the chests.”
sentences.i: —“With pleasure,” said the Çid; “let it be promised from this moment, if I bring it you from over there; if not, reckon it against the chests.”
sentences.n: Plazme = pláceme, 'it pleases me' (plazer, 3rd sg. present + me). daquí = de aquí, 'from here' and so 'from now on'; sea mandada is a present subjunctive passive, and mandar here means 'to promise, to pledge', as it will in v. 224 (mando al vuestro altar …). aduxier is the future subjunctive of aducir 'to bring' on its strong preterite stem adux- (the form serves for first and third person singular; here 'if I bring'). dallá = de allá, 'from over there', the Moorish lands. contalda = contadla, imperative + la with the same -dl- > -ld- metathesis as prestalde and Levaldas (vv. 118, 167). The si-clause hangs on the promise before it: the fur is pledged if the Çid brings it back. contalda sobre las arcas, 'count it upon the chests', most likely means 'add its price to the debt secured on the chests' (sobre as at v. 161) — a joke the audience can enjoy and Raquel cannot, since the chests hold sand; the exact sense is not certain.

sentences.i: Raquel and Vidas carried off the chests, and Martín Antolínez rode into Burgos with them. With every precaution they reach the lenders' house;
sentences.n: These three lines are not in the manuscript: they are Pidal's restoration, printed wholly in italics and without numbers of their own, which fills the passage from the Çid's tent to the lenders' house (shown here in plain type). The letters b, c, d after 181 are ours, added so that the traditional count stays undisturbed, as with 14b in the opening tiradas. levavan, entrava: imperfects, and then llegan in the present — epic tense-mixing inside one sentence. con todo recabdo = 'with every precaution' (recabdo as in con grand recabdo, of the king's sealed letter at v. 24). la posada here is the lenders' own house in Burgos, not the Çid's lodging.

sentences.t:
en medio del palaçio tendieron un almoçalla,
sobrella una sávana de rançal e muy blanca.
sentences.l:
in middle of-the hall they-spread a rug,
upon-it a sheet of fine-linen and very white.
sentences.i: in the middle of the hall they spread a rug, and over it a sheet of fine linen, very white.
sentences.n: palaçio = the main hall of the house (as at v. 115), not a palace. almoçalla is an Arabic word (al-muṣallà, a prayer-mat), here a rug or floor-cloth; the masculine article un with a noun in -a is as the text has it. sobrella = sobre ella. rançal is a fine linen cloth. The white sheet is a counting-cloth: the coin is to be poured out and reckoned on it in full view.

sentences.t:
A tod el primer colpe trezientos marcos de plata,
notólos don Martino, sin peso los tomava;
los otros trezientos en oro gelos pagavan.
Çinco escuderos tiene don Martino, a todos los cargava.
sentences.l:
At all the first stroke three-hundred marks of silver,
counted-them don Martino, without weight them he-was-taking;
the other three-hundred in gold them-to-him they-were-paying.
Five squires has don Martino, all of-them he-was-loading.
sentences.i: At the very first stroke, three hundred marks of silver: don Martino counted them, taking them without weighing; the other three hundred they paid him in gold. Don Martino has five squires with him, and he loaded every one of them.
sentences.n: tod el = todo el, 'the very'; colpe = golpe, so a tod el primer colpe = 'at the very first go', without haggling. don Martino is Martín Antolínez, under a fuller form of his name with the honorific don (so again at vv. 199 and 232). notólos = los notó, 'he counted them, took note of them'; sin peso, 'without weighing' — the mark was a weight of silver, so to take the coin by tale alone is a show of trust, matching the trust the lenders have placed in the unopened chests. gelos = ge los, 'them to him', as at v. 136. Tense-mixing again: notó (preterite), tomava, pagavan, cargava (imperfects) and tiene (present). The six hundred marks of v. 135 come half in silver and half in gold.

sentences.i: When he had done this — you shall hear what he said: “Ah, don Raquel and Vidas, the chests are in your hands; and I, who won you this, have well deserved a pair of hose.”
sentences.n: ovo fecho is the preterite anterior, aver in the preterite + participle, 'when he had done'; fecho = hecho, initial f- again. odredes = oiréis, the minstrel's aside to his listeners, as at v. 70. mereçía is the imperfect of mereçer used modestly, 'I would deserve, I have surely earned'. calças are hose, the cloth leg-coverings of the period: to ask for 'hose' is to ask for a go-between's commission in the form of a garment, and the lenders take the hint at once in the next tirada.

sentences.t:
Entre Raquel e Vidas aparte ixieron amos:
“démosle buen don, ca él no' lo ha buscado.
sentences.l:
Between Raquel and Vidas apart went-out both:
“let-us-give-him good gift, for he to-us it has procured.
sentences.i: Raquel and Vidas stepped aside together, the two of them: “Let us give him a good gift, for it is he who has found this for us.
sentences.n: Tirada 11 (assonance á-o) — the lenders give Martín Antolínez thirty marks; he rides back to the Çid's tent, reports the six hundred, and urges him to strike camp for San Pedro de Cardeña. The á-o holds through the whole tirada (amos, buscado, contado … vassallo, algo … plaz[d]o); nasco (v. 202) and dalgo (v. 210) fit it too, the a stressed and the o final. ixieron is the preterite of exir 'to go out' (cf. exien, v. 16); entre … amos = 'the two of them together'. démosle, hortative present subjunctive + le, 'let us give him'. no' = nos, its s lost before the l (Pidal's apostrophe marks the dropped letter): no' lo ha buscado, 'he has procured it for us' (buscar = 'to obtain, bring about'), i.e. he got us this business. The sense of buscar here is the likeliest one, not a certain one.

sentences.t:
Martín Antolínez, un Burgalés contado,
vos lo mereçedes, darvos queremos buen dado,
de que fagades calças e rica piel e buen manto.
sentences.l:
Martín Antolínez, a Burgalese renowned,
you it deserve, to-give-you we-want good gift,
from which you-may-make hose and rich fur and good mantle.
sentences.i: Martín Antolínez, renowned man of Burgos, you deserve it: we mean to give you a handsome gift, enough to make yourself hose and a rich fur and a good mantle.
sentences.n: un Burgalés contado: contado, 'reckoned, renowned', was the Campeador's epithet in the last tirada (vv. 142, 152); the lenders now bestow it on his go-between. dado = 'a gift', the past participle of dar used as a noun. fagades, present subjunctive of fazer, 'that you may make'. The lenders outbid the request: Martín Antolínez asked for hose, and they offer hose, fur and mantle — a full suit of clothes.

sentences.i: We give you thirty marks as a gift; you will make it up to us, as is only right, and you will stand by us in what we have agreed.”
sentences.n: Dámosvos … a vos: the person is marked twice, enclitic vos and a vos, as a mio Çid … besáronle at v. 159. hedes = avedes, the 2nd pl. present of aver worn down, and mereçer no' lo hedes, atorgar nos hedes are split futures (= nos lo mereceréis, nos otorgaréis), the same construction as doblar vos he and pedir vos a in the last part. no' is again nos. The sense of both lines is uncertain: mereçer can mean 'to deserve' or 'to earn back, repay', and atorgar 'to grant, confirm, vouch for'. Together they seem to ask Martín Antolínez, in return for the thirty marks, to stand by the bargain just struck (esto que avemos parado, 'this we have settled', cf. el pleyto a parado, v. 160) — the gift as a retainer.

sentences.t:
Gradeçiólo don Martino e recibió los marcos;
gradó exir de la posada e espidiós de amos.
sentences.l:
Thanked-it don Martino and received the marks;
he-was-glad to-go-out from the house and took-leave-himself of both.
sentences.i: Don Martino thanked them and took the marks; he was glad to be out of the house, and took his leave of them both.
sentences.n: Gradeçiólo = lo agradeció. gradó is the preterite of gradar 'to be glad, take pleasure' (cf. Grádanse, v. 172), so 'he was glad to leave' — either pleasure at a good night's work or relief at getting away before the lenders look more closely; the poem does not say which. espidiós = espidióse, 'took his leave' (espedirse = despedirse), the -se worn to -s after the stressed vowel as in tornós and Sonrrisós.

sentences.t:
Exido es de Burgos e Arlançón, a passado,
vino pora la tienda del que en buen ora nasco.
sentences.l:
Gone-out he-is from Burgos and Arlançón, he-has crossed,
he-came toward the tent of-the-one who in good hour was-born.
sentences.i: He is out of Burgos, he has crossed the Arlanzón, and he came to the tent of him who was born in a good hour.
sentences.n: Exido es = 'he has gone out': verbs of motion form the perfect with ser, not aver (es exido like French il est sorti), while passar takes aver (a passado = ha pasado) in the same line. Arlançón, the river of Burgos (v. 55), stands as the fronted object of a passado. del que en buen ora nasco: the birth-form of the formula, 'born in a good hour'; nasco is the strong preterite of nasçer, 'was born' (= nació).

sentences.t:
Reçibiólo el Çid abiertos amos los braços:
“¿Venides, Martín Antolínez, el mio fi[d]el vassallo!
Aun vea el dia que de mí ayades algo!”
sentences.l:
Received-him the Çid open both the arms:
“You-come, Martín Antolínez, the my faithful vassal!
Yet may-I-see the day that from me you-may-have something!”
sentences.i: The Çid received him with both arms open: “You are come, Martín Antolínez, my faithful vassal! May I yet live to see the day when you have something from me!”
sentences.n: abiertos amos los braços is an absolute phrase, 'both arms open' (amos = ambos). ¿Venides …! — Pidal opens with a question mark and closes with an exclamation: a greeting half question, half cry. Venides = venís. el mio fi[d]el vassallo, article + possessive again, with the d restored by Pidal. vea is a present subjunctive of wish, 'may I see'; ayades = hayáis, present subjunctive of aver. algo is again 'something of value, wealth' (vv. 111, 157): the Çid, penniless for now, wishes Martín Antolínez the reward he has not yet had.

sentences.t:
—“Vengo, Campeador, con todo buen recabdo:
vos seysçientos e yo treynta he ganados.
sentences.l:
—“I-come, Campeador, with all good outcome:
you six-hundred and I thirty have gained.
sentences.i: —“I come, Campeador, with everything well in hand: you have gained six hundred, and I thirty.
sentences.n: recabdo (modern recaudo) here is the business done and secured, 'with everything safely accomplished'. he ganados: a single aver serves both subjects, and the participle agrees with the marks understood (plural). The thirty marks are reported at once: Martín Antolínez keeps nothing back from his lord.

sentences.i: Have the tent struck and let us be off quickly: let the cock crow for us at San Pedro de Cardeña. We shall see your wife, that wise and well-born lady.
sentences.n: Mandad coger la tienda: coger is 'to take up', so 'have the tent struck' (as the narrator says it is done at v. 213). vayamos, hortative subjunctive; cante, present subjunctive of wish, with i = 'there' (Latin ibi). San Pero (= San Pedro) de Cardeña is a Benedictine monastery a few miles south-east of Burgos; the Çid's wife is waiting there. The cockcrow is the deadline set at v. 169 (ante que cante el gallo). menbrada, 'prudent, sensible' (cf. a guisa de menbrado, vv. 102, 131). fija dalgo = hija de algo, 'daughter of something', i.e. of good family — the phrase that became hidalgo.

sentences.t:
Mesuraremos la posada e quitaremos el reynado;
mucho es huebos, ca çerca viene el plaz[d]o.”
sentences.l:
We-shall-measure the lodging and we-shall-quit the kingdom;
much is need, for near comes the term.”
sentences.i: We shall keep our stay there short, and leave the kingdom; there is great need of it, for the term is drawing near.”
sentences.n: Mesuraremos la posada is uncertain. mesurar is 'to measure, to keep within measure', so 'we shall measure out our lodging' most probably means 'keep our stop at Cardeña short'; 'we shall set our stay in order' is also possible, but the pairing with quitaremos el reynado and the haste of the next line favour a curtailed visit. quitar = 'to leave, quit' (D'aquí quito Castiella, v. 219), and el reynado is the realm itself. Both are simple futures (the synthetic form), beside the split futures of v. 197–198. mucho es huebos = 'it is very needful' (huebos again, vv. 83, 123, 138). el plaz[d]o (= plazo, the d restored by Pidal) is the time-limit set on the Çid's departure from the kingdom.

sentences.t:
Estas palabras dichas, la tienda es cogida.
Mio Çid e sus conpañas, cavalgan tan aína.
sentences.l:
These words said, the tent is struck.
My Çid and his companies, they-mount so swiftly.
sentences.i: These words spoken, the tent is struck. My Çid and his companies mount, and swiftly.
sentences.n: Tirada 12 (assonance í-a) — the Çid turns his horse toward Santa María of Burgos and prays to the Virgin, promising a thousand masses if she brings him through. Every ending carries í-a: cogida, aína, María, santigua, guías … missas (santigua is stressed santígua, with -ua as its final vowel; aína is a-í-na). Estas palabras dichas is an absolute participle phrase, like la oraçión fecha at v. 54; es cogida is the passive present, 'is taken up'. tan aína = 'very quickly' (aína, 'swiftly'). The comma after conpañas separates subject from verb, as Pidal prints it.

sentences.t:
La cara del cavallo tornó a Santa María,
alçó su mano diestra, la cara se santigua:
sentences.l:
The face of-the horse he-turned to Santa María,
he-raised his hand right, the face himself he-crosses:
sentences.i: He turned his horse's head toward Santa María, raised his right hand, and crosses himself:
sentences.n: Santa María is the cathedral of Burgos where he prayed at v. 52; he turns the horse to face it for a last farewell. la cara se santigua = 'he signs his face with the cross' (santiguarse). Preterites tornó, alçó, then the present santigua: tense-mixing once more.

sentences.t:
“A tí lo gradesco, Dios, que çielo e tierra guías;
válanme tus vertudes, gloriosa santa María!
sentences.l:
“To thee it I-give-thanks, God, who heaven and earth guidest;
may-aid-me thy powers, glorious holy Mary!
sentences.i: “To thee I give thanks for it, God, who guidest heaven and earth; may thy powers aid me, glorious Saint Mary!
sentences.n: gradesco = agradezco, 1st sg. present. válanme is the present subjunctive of valer, plural to agree with tus vertudes, with me glued on: 'may thy powers avail me' (cf. vala, v. 48). The prayer opens to God and turns at once to the Virgin; tus vertudes here belong to Mary, the vocative of the line. vertudes = virtudes, 'miraculous powers', not moral virtues.

sentences.t:
D'aquí quito Castiella, pues que el rey he en ira;
non sé si entraré y más en todos los mios días.
sentences.l:
From-here I-quit Castile, since the king I-have in wrath;
not I-know if I-shall-enter there more in all the my days.
sentences.i: From here I leave Castile, since the king's wrath is upon me; I do not know whether I shall come back into it again in all my days.
sentences.n: D'aquí = de aquí; quito, 1st sg. present of quitar 'to leave'. el rey he en ira, 'I have the king in wrath' — aver as a full verb, 'to hold, to have', and ira once again the legal state of royal disgrace (v. 74). y = 'there' (= allí, French y). los mios días, article + possessive.

sentences.t:
Vuestra vertud me vala, Gloriosa, en mi exida
e me ayude [e] me acorra de noch e de día!
sentences.l:
Your power me may-aid, Glorious-one, in my going-out
and me may-help [and] me may-succour by night and by day!
sentences.i: May your power aid me, Glorious Lady, in my going forth, and help me and succour me by night and by day!
sentences.n: The Çid has passed from tú (tus vertudes, v. 218) to vos (vuestra vertud) within four lines, both addressed to the Virgin: the poem uses either as the line requires. vala, ayude, acorra are present subjunctives of wish; acorrer = socorrer, 'to succour'. exida = salida, the leaving of the land (cf. v. 11). noch = noche. The [e] is Pidal's restoration.

sentences.i: If you do so, and my fortune turns out well for me, I promise to your altar good gifts and rich ones; and this I bind myself to as a debt, to have a thousand masses sung there.”
sentences.n: fiziéredes (2nd pl.) and f[o]re (3rd sg.) are future subjunctives of fazer and ser, the normal mood of an open condition in Old Spanish (cf. f[o]re, v. 92); fiziéredes has initial f- for modern h-. complida = cumplida, 'fulfilled'. mando, 'I promise, I vow', the sense of mandar at v. 180. al vuestro altar, article + possessive. donas = 'gifts, offerings' (Latin dona). [h]e yo en debdo, 'I hold it as a debt' (debdo = deuda): aver as a full verb again, h restored by Pidal. faga … cantar, 'that I have sung' — fazer + infinitive as causative. i = 'there', at Santa María. A vow of masses for success in exile is a pious bargain, and the poem plainly presents it as one.

sentences.t:
Spidiós el caboso de cuer e de veluntad.
Sueltan las riendas e pienssan de aguijar.
sentences.l:
Took-leave-himself the excellent-one with heart and with will.
They-loosen the reins and set-about to-spur.
sentences.i: The worthy man took his leave with all his heart and will. They slacken the reins and set spur to their horses.
sentences.n: Tirada 13 (assonance á) — the leave-taking; Martín Antolínez will go back to Burgos for a moment and rejoin before sunrise. This tirada rhymes on a single stressed á (veluntad, aguijar, [leal], solaz, far, incal, rayar — leal in Pidal's restoration), the masculine ending, with nothing after the vowel to count. Spidiós = espidióse, with the initial e- dropped (cf. espidiós, v. 200). caboso = 'accomplished, excellent' (from cabo 'end, completion'). Who the caboso is, is uncertain: elsewhere the epithet belongs to the Çid, and he has just ended his farewell to Santa María; but the next lines turn at once to Martín Antolínez parting from the company, and the phrase may be his leave-taking. de cuer e de veluntad, 'from heart and will', a doubled formula like de voluntad e de grado (v. 149); cuer = corazón (Latin cor). v. 227 repeats v. 10 with its halves reversed (Allí pienssan de aguijar, allí sueltan las riendas): pensar de + infinitive, 'set about'.

sentences.t:
Dixo Martín Antolínez, [el Burgalés leal]:
“veré a la mugier a todo mio solaz,
castigar los he commo abrán a far.
sentences.l:
Said Martín Antolínez, [the Burgalese loyal]:
“I-shall-see the wife at all my ease,
to-instruct them I-will how they-will-have to do.
sentences.i: Martín Antolínez, the loyal man of Burgos, said: “I shall see my wife, to my heart's content, and I shall instruct my household how they are to manage.
sentences.n: The whole second half of v. 228, [el Burgalés leal], is Pidal's restoration. The next line is numbered 228b in his edition, keeping the traditional count. la mugier = 'my wife', the article doing the work of a possessive. a todo mio solaz, 'at all my comfort', to his heart's content — though the visit is short, for he is to be back before dawn. castigar los he = los castigaré, the split future (los, his household), with castigar in its old sense 'to instruct, admonish', not 'to punish'. abrán a far = habrán de hacer: aver a + infinitive for obligation (cf. a mover [h]a, v. 169), with far, the short form of fazer, as fer at v. 84.

sentences.t:
Si el rey me lo quisiere tomar, a mi non m'incal.
Antes seré convusco que el sol quiera rayar.”
sentences.l:
If the king to-me it should-wish to-take, to me not to-me-it-matters.
Before I-shall-be with-you than the sun may-wish to-shine.”
sentences.i: If the king chooses to take it from me, it is nothing to me. I shall be with you before the sun is ready to rise.”
sentences.n: quisiere is the future subjunctive of querer; lo is everything Martín Antolínez owns, forfeit for helping the exile (he foresaw it at vv. 73–74). a mi non m'incal = 'it does not matter to me': incal is the 3rd sg. present of incaler 'to concern, to matter', with its final -e lost, and the person marked twice (a mi … m'). Antes … que, 'sooner … than'. convusco = 'with you' (cf. convus[c]o, v. 168). quiera rayar: querer + infinitive in the sense 'to be about to', 'before the sun starts to shine'; rayar = to send out rays.

sentences.t:
Tornavas [don] Martin[o] a Burgos e mio Çid aguij[ó]
pora San Pero de Cardeña quanto pudo a espol[ón],
con estos cavalleros quel sirven a so sabor.
sentences.l:
Was-turning-himself [don] Martino to Burgos and my Çid spurred
toward San Pero of Cardeña as-much-as he-could at spur,
with these knights who-him serve at his pleasure.
sentences.i: Don Martino turned back toward Burgos, and my Çid spurred on for San Pedro de Cardeña as hard as he could ride, with these knights who serve him at his pleasure.
sentences.n: Tirada 14 (assonance ó) — the Çid reaches San Pedro de Cardeña at cockcrow, where the abbot is at matins and doña Ximena is praying for him. The tirada rhymes on stressed ó (aguij[ó], espol[ón], sabor, Campeador, Criador, pro), and twice on ó-e (albores, vv. 235 and 238); the epic treats ó and ó-e as one assonance, the final -e being optional, as the paragogic -e of tirada 3 showed. In aguij[ó] and espol[ón] the bracketed endings, at the rhyme-word itself, are Pidal's restorations. Tornavas = tornávase, imperfect + reflexive. [don] and the -o of Martin[o] are Pidal's, giving the name the form it had at vv. 185, 187, 199. a espol[ón], 'at the spur', at full gallop. quel = que le; so = su. a so sabor = 'at his pleasure, as he wishes'.

sentences.t:
Apriessa cantan los gallos e quieren [cr]ebar albores,
quando llegó a San Pero el buen Campeador;
sentences.l:
In-haste sing the cocks and want to-break dawns,
when arrived at San Pero the good Campeador;
sentences.i: The cocks are crowing thick and fast and the dawn is about to break when the good Campeador came to San Pedro;
sentences.n: Apriessa, 'hurriedly, thick and fast'. The cockcrow Martín Antolínez wished for at v. 209 is here on time. quieren [cr]ebar: querer + infinitive as 'be about to', as in quiera rayar at v. 231. [cr]ebar = quebrar 'to break', its cr restored by Pidal: 'the dawns are about to break'. albores, plural, are the first lights of day (again at v. 238). Present cantan, quieren beside preterite llegó: epic tense-mixing at the moment of arrival. The Campeador spelling here has m, against Canpeador at v. 175 — the copyist uses both.

sentences.t:
el abbat don Sancho, cristiano del Criador;
rezaba los matines abuelta de los albores.
sentences.l:
the abbot don Sancho, Christian of-the Creator,
was-saying the matins at-the-turn of the dawns.
sentences.i: the abbot, don Sancho, a Christian of the Creator, was saying matins at the break of day.
sentences.n: Pidal's semicolon after Criador is a pause, not a full stop: el abbat don Sancho is the subject of rezaba. cristiano del Criador, 'Christian of the Creator', i.e. a true servant of God — a praising epithet. los matines, the night office, sung before dawn; rezaba is spelt with b here, as the edition prints it. abuelta de = 'together with, at the same time as' (a vuelta de), so 'with the dawn'.

sentences.t:
Y estava doña Ximena con çinco dueñas de pro,
rogando a San Pero e al Criador:
“Tú que a todos guías, val a mio Çid el Campeador.”
sentences.l:
There was doña Ximena with five ladies of worth,
praying to San Pero and to-the Creator:
“Thou who all guidest, aid my Çid the Campeador.”
sentences.i: There too was doña Ximena, with five ladies of worth, praying to Saint Peter and to the Creator: “Thou who guidest all, aid my Çid the Campeador.”
sentences.n: Y = 'there' (= allí), not 'and'. doña Ximena (x = sh), the Çid's wife, is named here for the first time, met at prayer. dueñas = ladies, married women of her household; de pro, 'of worth, of standing'. rogando, a bare gerund, 'praying', the prayer of the wife answering the Çid's own at vv. 217–225. val is the imperative of valer, final -e lost, 'aid, protect'; guías echoes the Çid's que çielo e tierra guías (v. 217). Ximena too calls him mio Çid — the epithet is in everyone's mouth, not only the narrator's.
